# How to use this guide

Quality Control and Standardization of Herbals (BP806ET) is a **semester-8 elective** of the PCI B.Pharm course. It has no practical paper. It builds on Pharmacognosy (semesters 4 and 5) and Herbal Drug Technology (semester 6), so revise the evaluation of crude drugs and Schedule T from those subjects first. This subject is mostly **guidelines, definitions, lists and tables** — WHO, EU, ICH and Indian law — plus the standard quality control tests and chromatographic methods. Marks come from writing the right name of each guideline, its headings in order, and one or two examples for each point.

The five units follow the five units of the PCI syllabus exactly. Unit 4 is the most mixed (stability testing, chromatography, new drug and export dossiers, and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act); study it on two days — science on one day, documents and law on the next.

Study one unit a day: read the notes, write the "Remember" list from memory, then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short answer (5-mark) and long essay (10-mark) questions, rated by how often that kind of question appears in PCI-syllabus pharmacy papers.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ questions — all 20 | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

The app's full mock paper follows this pattern, and a 20-question, 20-minute quick MCQ test is also given.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with headings, a table or flow chart, and examples.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 WHO quality control | WHO guidelines for quality control of herbal drugs (all parameters), sampling, ash and extractive values, foaming and swelling index, contaminants and their limits, evaluation methods and adulteration of crude drugs, basic tests for drugs |
| 2 Quality assurance | WHO GACP for medicinal plants, WHO GMP for herbal medicines, GLP principles, Schedule T, specification of a herbal material |
| 3 EU and ICH | Traditional herbal registration (Directive 2004/24/EC), well-established use, EU extract types, ICH guidelines applied to herbals, WHO research guidelines for safety and efficacy |
| 4 Stability and chromatography | Stability testing of herbal products and climatic zones, HPTLC fingerprinting, HPLC and GC uses, method validation, dossier for new drug and export registration, Chapter IV-A provisions |
| 5 Regulation and markers | WHO pharmacovigilance guidelines for herbal medicines, comparison of herbal pharmacopoeias, chemical and DNA markers with examples |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Name the guideline in full on the first line ("WHO guidelines on Good Agricultural and Collection Practices for medicinal plants") — it shows the examiner you know the source.
2. Write guideline answers as **numbered headings** in the order of the document (for GACP: identification → seeds → cultivation → harvest → collection → processing → packaging → storage → personnel → documentation). Each heading with one line earns more than a long paragraph.
3. Draw a **flow chart** wherever there is a sequence: sampling and quartering, stability protocol, HPTLC steps, field-to-factory traceability, pharmacovigilance reporting.
4. Learn the **numbers that are safe to quote**: WHO sampling (all up to 5; 5 from 6–50; 10% above 50), foreign-matter sample sizes (500/250/50 g), total ash at 500–600 °C, foaming index = 1000/a, WHO lead 10 mg/kg and cadmium 0.3 mg/kg, ICH 40 °C/75% RH accelerated, India zone IVb 30 °C/75% RH, EU traditional use 30 years (15 in the EU). If you are not sure of a number, describe the rule without it.
5. Give **plant examples** with every marker or test: sennosides (senna), withaferin A (ashwagandha), curcumin (turmeric), glycyrrhizin (liquorice), swelling index (isabgol), bitterness value (chirata, gentian).
6. Do not confuse: quality assurance vs GMP vs quality control; GAP vs GACP vs GMP vs GLP vs GCP; standardised vs quantified extracts; active vs analytical markers; well-established use vs traditional use; ASU DTAB (33C) vs ASU DCC (33D); Schedule T (GMP) vs Schedule E(1) (poisonous ASU drugs).
7. Finish regulatory answers with one line on **why it matters to India** — exports, Ministry of AYUSH, WHO-GMP certification.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you only have an hour, learn these five answers with headings and a diagram: **WHO guidelines for quality control of herbal drugs**, **WHO GACP for medicinal plants**, **stability testing of herbal medicines**, **HPTLC fingerprinting and markers**, and **WHO pharmacovigilance guidelines for herbal medicines**. Add **EU traditional herbal registration** as the sixth if time allows.

## Unit 1 — Basic tests and WHO quality control

- Quality = **identity + purity + content**, plus safety and batch consistency.
- WHO **Basic tests for drugs**: substances, plant materials, dosage forms; simple tests to confirm identity and detect gross degradation; **never replace** pharmacopoeial tests.
- WHO **QC methods for medicinal plant materials** (1998) → **for herbal materials** (2011): a methods manual, not a pharmacopoeia.
- **Sampling**: ≤5 containers — all; 6–50 — 5; >50 — 10% (rounded up to a multiple of 10); top, middle, bottom; quartering; retain a reference sample.
- **Foreign matter** sample: 500 g roots/bark, 250 g leaves/flowers/seeds/fruit, 50 g cut material.
- **Ash**: total (500–600 °C), acid-insoluble (silica/sand), water-soluble (low in exhausted drug), sulphated.
- **Extractives**: hot (reflux 1 h) and cold (6 h + 18 h maceration); 25 ml filtrate dried at 105 °C.
- **Water**: toluene distillation (water only); LOD at 100–105 °C (water + volatiles).
- **Bitterness**: vs quinine hydrochloride (1 g in 2000 ml = 1 unit). **Foaming index** = 1000/a. **Swelling index** = ml per g. **Tannins** with hide powder. **Haemolytic activity** vs saponin.
- **Contaminants**: pesticides (GC; limits from ADI), arsenic and toxic metals (AAS/ICP), microbes, aflatoxins (HPLC-fluorescence), radioactivity.
- **Limits**: WHO gives no single global limits, only national examples. WHO-suggested **lead 10 mg/kg, cadmium 0.3 mg/kg**. Microbial example: teas/topical aerobic bacteria 10^7/g, other internal herbal materials 10^5/g; *Salmonella*, *Shigella* absent. Aflatoxin example (Germany): B1 2 µg/kg, total 4 µg/kg.
- Limits from data: about 20 batches, mean ± 3 SD.
- **Evaluation**: organoleptic, microscopic (stomatal index = S×100/(E+S), palisade ratio, vein-islet and vein-termination number, lycopodium spore method), physical, chemical, chromatographic, biological.
- **Adulteration**: inferior varieties, exhausted drug, look-alike plants, artificial material, synthetic principles, wrong parts, heavy matter, spoiled drug.

## Unit 2 — Quality assurance

- QA ⊃ GMP ⊃ QC; cGMP = current GMP.
- **WHO GACP (2003)**: identification + voucher specimen, seeds, site, climate/soil, irrigation/fertiliser, crop protection, harvest, wild collection (permits, sustainability), primary processing (drying), packaging/labelling, storage/transport, equipment, personnel, documentation, QA, ethics. NMPB GACP in India.
- **WHO GMP for herbal medicines (2007)** — supplementary: separate raw-herb store, dust extraction, quarantine, voucher/reference samples, fingerprint specs, contaminant testing, validated processes.
- Herbal specification: botanical name, source, part, description, identity (TLC), assay, purity, contaminants, storage. Extracts add solvent, DER, residual solvents.
- **Schedule T**: Part I GMP headings; Part II machinery and minimum area. Schedule E(1) poisonous ASU drugs.
- **GLP** (OECD): study director, QA unit, facilities, apparatus, test systems, test items, SOPs, study plan, reporting, archives. India: NGCMA (DST).

## Unit 3 — EU, ICH and research guidelines

- EMA → **HMPC**; Directive 2001/83/EC; **Directive 2004/24/EC** (traditional registration).
- Routes: full; **well-established use** (≥10 years in EU, literature); **traditional use** (30 years incl. 15 in EU; oral/external/inhalation; no medical supervision; full quality data).
- EU herbal monographs and the EU list.
- Extracts: **standardised** (known actives, fixed value), **quantified** (active markers, range), **other** (analytical markers). DER = herb : extract.
- ICH: Q1A(R2) stability, Q1B photostability, Q2 validation, Q3C residual solvents, Q3D elemental impurities, Q6A approach, Q7, Q8–Q10, M4 CTD, S-series, E6 GCP. No herbal-only ICH guideline.
- WHO research guidelines: quality first; traditional use is evidence; new preparation/indication needs new data; acute → repeated-dose → special toxicity; GLP; clinical phases I–IV, ethics, GCP; placebo and individualised-treatment problems.

## Unit 4 — Stability, chromatography, dossiers, law

- Herbal stability: marker + **fingerprint** + physical + microbial + dosage-form tests.
- Zones: I 21/45 · II 25/60 · III 30/35 · IVa 30/65 · **IVb 30/75 (India)**. Accelerated 40/75 for 6 months (0, 3, 6). Long-term 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 18, 24 months then yearly. Rule 161-B shelf life of ASU drugs.
- Fingerprint = pattern of bands/peaks; Rf = spot ÷ solvent front.
- HPTLC: application → development (twin trough) → derivatisation → densitometry. HPLC: C18, PDA, marker assay. GC: oils, pesticides, solvents. LC–MS/GC–MS: unknowns and adulterants.
- ICH Q2 validation: specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision, LOD, LOQ, robustness.
- India: classical ASU (textual reference), proprietary ASU (safety + effectiveness, Rule 158-B), **phytopharmaceutical** (≥4 defined compounds; CDSCO, NDCT Rules 2019).
- Export: licence, GMP/WHO-GMP, COPP/free sale certificate, dossier (CTD), CoA, stability, heavy metal/pesticide/microbial/aflatoxin reports, biodiversity/CITES clearance, Pharmexcil.
- Chapter IV-A: 33C ASU DTAB, 33D ASU DCC, 33E misbranded, 33EE adulterated, 33EEA spurious, 33EEC prohibition. Rule 161 labelling.

## Unit 5 — Regulation, pharmacovigilance, pharmacopoeias, markers

- Regulation: quality, safety, efficacy, labelling, post-marketing. USA DSHEA 1994 (supplements) vs botanical drug; Canada NHP; Australia listed/registered; China TCM volume.
- **WHO PV guidelines for herbal medicines (2004)**: include herbs in national systems; report botanical name, part, preparation, batch, source, sample; product analysis; WHO–UMC causality; Uppsala Monitoring Centre. Issues: identity (aristolochia), adulteration, interactions (St John's wort), multi-herb products.
- India: PvPI (IPC); AYUSH pharmacovigilance (AIIA New Delhi) + misleading advertisements.
- Pharmacopoeias: API (Part I single drugs, Part II formulations, PCIM&H), UPI, SPI, HPI, IP, IHP (IDMA + RRL Jammu), BHP, Ph. Eur., USP, Chinese, Japanese; WHO monographs advisory; Commission E/ESCOP therapeutic.
- Indian limits: Pb 10 ppm, Hg 1 ppm, As 3 ppm, Cd 0.3 ppm.
- **Markers**: active, analytical, negative. Senna–sennosides; turmeric–curcumin; ashwagandha–withaferin A; liquorice–glycyrrhizin; brahmi–bacosides; kalmegh–andrographolide; vasaka–vasicine; guggul–guggulsterones; pepper–piperine.
- **Biological markers**: bioassays, isoenzymes, DNA (RAPD, RFLP, AFLP, SSR, SCAR, barcoding ITS2/rbcL/matK). DNA = identity, not quality.

questions.answer:
1. Source: WHO 'Quality control methods for medicinal plant materials' (1998), updated as 'Quality control methods for herbal materials' (2011) — a manual of test methods for national standards, not a pharmacopoeia.
2. Sampling: up to 5 containers sample all; 6–50 sample 5; above 50 sample 10%; three samples (top, middle, bottom); pooled sample reduced by quartering; retained reference sample.
3. Identity: macroscopy (shape, size, colour, fracture, odour, taste), microscopy (stomata, trichomes, crystals, starch), TLC fingerprint against a reference.
4. Purity: foreign matter (500 g roots/bark, 250 g leaves/seeds, 50 g cut material); total ash at 500–600 °C, acid-insoluble ash (sand), water-soluble ash; extractive values (hot and cold); water by toluene distillation and loss on drying.
5. Special tests: volatile oil, bitterness value (quinine hydrochloride reference), haemolytic activity, tannins (hide powder), swelling index, foaming index (1000/a).
6. Safety (contaminants): pesticide residues (GC), arsenic and toxic metals (AAS/ICP), microbial contamination (total viable count, E. coli, Salmonella), aflatoxins B1, B2, G1, G2 (HPLC with fluorescence), radioactive contamination.
7. Limits: WHO cannot recommend single international limits; gives examples of national limits; WHO-suggested lead 10 mg/kg, cadmium 0.3 mg/kg; microbial examples (teas/topical aerobic bacteria 10^7/g; other internal herbal materials 10^5/g; Salmonella absent).
8. Limits from data: grand mean ± 3 SD of about 20 batches.
9. Significance: uniform quality, detection of adulteration, patient safety, export acceptance.
questions.question: Describe the WHO guidelines for quality control of herbal drugs. Mention the parameters used to assess identity, purity and safety of herbal materials.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: debasement of a crude drug by admixture, substitution or removal of constituents, deliberate or accidental.
2. Reasons: scarcity, high price, confusion of vernacular names, ignorance of authentic plant, careless collection and storage.
3. Types: substitution with inferior commercial varieties (Indian for Alexandrian senna); exhausted drug (extracted ginger, clove); superficially similar cheaper plants or wrong parts; artificially manufactured material (imitation nutmeg); addition of synthetic principles (synthetic citral in lemon oil); worthless heavy materials (sand, stones); harmful or spoiled drug (mouldy, insect-infested).
4. Organoleptic evaluation: colour, odour, taste, size, shape, surface, fracture.
5. Microscopic: sections and powder; histochemical tests; quantitative microscopy — stomatal number and index, palisade ratio, vein-islet and vein-termination number, lycopodium spore method.
6. Physical: moisture, ash values, extractive values, swelling and foaming index, viscosity, refractive index, optical rotation, melting point.
7. Chemical: identity tests (Borntrager's for anthraquinones), assays, acid/saponification values.
8. Chromatographic and spectroscopic: TLC/HPTLC fingerprint, HPLC marker assay.
9. Biological: bioassay when chemistry is inadequate.
10. Conclusion: a combination of methods is needed; each detects different kinds of adulteration.
questions.question: What is adulteration of crude drugs? Classify the types of adulteration with examples and describe the methods used to evaluate commercial crude drugs.

questions.answer:
1. Basic tests for drugs: WHO volumes for pharmaceutical substances, medicinal plant materials and dosage forms.
2. Purpose: confirm identity when full analysis is not possible; detect gross degradation; screen suspect samples in the supply chain.
3. Features: simple reagents and apparatus, short tests with clear results, can be done by a trained pharmacist outside a full laboratory.
4. Tests — substances: appearance, solubility, colour/precipitation reactions, melting behaviour, simple TLC; plant materials: macroscopy, odour/taste, microscopy, simple chemical tests, UV fluorescence, TLC; dosage forms: visual inspection, identity reaction, simple disintegration, signs of degradation.
5. Difference: basic tests only confirm identity/gross quality; pharmacopoeial tests give full identity, purity and assay with limits and validated methods. A sample passing a basic test is not proven to be of pharmacopoeial quality; failures must be sent for full analysis.
6. Contaminant tests: pesticide residues (organochlorine, organophosphorus, pyrethroids by GC; limits from ADI and daily intake of the herb); heavy metals (lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury by AAS/ICP; WHO-suggested lead 10 mg/kg, cadmium 0.3 mg/kg); microbes (TVC, yeasts and moulds, E. coli, Salmonella, S. aureus); aflatoxins (B1, B2, G1, G2; HPLC with fluorescence; test materials with history of contamination); radioactivity after nuclear accidents.
questions.question: Explain the WHO 'Basic tests for drugs'. How do they differ from pharmacopoeial tests? Add a note on tests for contaminants in herbal materials.

questions.answer:
1. Total ash: 2–4 g drug ignited at 500–600 °C until carbon-free; includes physiological ash (from plant tissue) and non-physiological ash (adhering earth).
2. Acid-insoluble ash: total ash boiled with dilute HCl, residue ignited; measures silica — sand and soil.
3. Water-soluble ash: total ash boiled with water; loss in weight; low in exhausted drugs.
4. Sulphated ash: after treatment with sulphuric acid; used for some drugs.
5. Significance: detect earthy adulteration, exhausted drug, careless collection; part of identity and purity specification.
questions.question: Write a note on ash values and their significance in evaluation of crude drugs.

questions.answer:
1. Inspect each container for labelling, damage and moisture; sample damaged containers separately.
2. Number to sample: up to 5 containers — all; 6–50 — 5; more than 50 — 10%, rounded up to the nearest multiple of 10.
3. Take three original samples from top, middle and bottom (first at least 10 cm deep in sacks; grain probe for seeds).
4. Combine into a pooled sample and mix.
5. Reduce by quartering: square heap, divide diagonally, keep two opposite quarters, repeat.
6. Divide the average sample into final samples for testing (fragmentation, identity, impurities, moisture, ash, actives) and keep a retained reference portion.
questions.question: Describe the WHO procedure for sampling of herbal materials.

questions.answer:
1. Foaming index: 1 g coarse powder boiled in 100 ml water for 30 min, filtered, made to 100 ml.
2. Pour 1, 2, 3 … 10 ml into 10 tubes, make each to 10 ml, shake lengthwise 15 s, stand 15 min, measure foam.
3. Index = 1000/a, where a = ml of decoction in the tube giving 1 cm foam; foam below 1 cm in all tubes means index below 100. Used for saponin drugs.
4. Swelling index: volume (ml) occupied by 1 g of drug after swelling in water.
5. Drug in a 25 ml stoppered cylinder with 25 ml water, shaken every 10 min for 1 h, stood 3 h; volume read; mean of at least three determinations. Used for isabgol, linseed, fenugreek.
questions.question: Explain the determination of foaming index and swelling index.

questions.answer:
1. Stomatal number: average stomata per sq mm of epidermis.
2. Stomatal index: SI = S × 100/(E + S); S = stomata, E = epidermal cells per unit area; constant for a species.
3. Palisade ratio: average palisade cells beneath one epidermal cell.
4. Vein-islet number: vein islets per sq mm of leaf; vein-termination number: vein endings per sq mm.
5. Lycopodium spore method: lycopodium spores (uniform size and number per mg) used as internal standard to find the percentage of a powdered drug or adulterant with countable elements.
6. Use: distinguish closely related species (Indian and Alexandrian senna), detect adulteration in powders.
questions.question: Write a note on quantitative microscopy (leaf constants).

questions.answer: The residue left after boiling the total ash with dilute hydrochloric acid and igniting; it measures silica, mainly sand and earthy matter adhering to the drug.
questions.question: What is acid-insoluble ash?

questions.answer: The bitterness of a herbal material compared with quinine hydrochloride; one unit equals the bitterness of a solution of 1 g quinine hydrochloride in 2000 ml. Used for bitters such as gentian and chirata.
questions.question: Define bitterness value.

questions.answer:
1. Published by WHO (2003); NMPB in India has issued GACP guidelines based on them.
2. Objectives: quality, safety and efficacy at the source; help national guidelines; sustainable cultivation and collection; respect for local communities.
3. Identification and authentication: botanical name and family, local names, voucher specimen in a herbarium.
4. Seeds and propagation material: authentic, pure, disease-free.
5. Cultivation: site free from heavy metals and pesticide residues; suitable climate and soil; clean irrigation water; composted manure; minimum, approved pesticides with records; integrated pest management.
6. Harvest: best season and time for constituents; dry weather; clean tools; no contact with soil.
7. Collection of wild plants: permits; no endangered species; sustainable methods; trained collectors.
8. Primary processing: inspection and sorting, washing if allowed, drying on clean surfaces protected from animals and dust, specific processing.
9. Packaging and labelling; storage and transport in dry, pest-proof stores; fumigation only with permitted agents.
10. Equipment, personnel (training, hygiene, protection), documentation for traceability, quality assurance, ethical and legal issues (benefit sharing, threatened species).
11. Benefits: consistent raw material, less contamination, traceability, export acceptance, conservation.

units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Basic tests, WHO guidelines for quality control and evaluation of crude drugs

A tablet of paracetamol contains one known molecule that can be assayed exactly. A herbal medicine contains a whole plant — or an extract of it — with hundreds of constituents, many of them unknown, and its make-up changes with the place it grew, the season it was collected and the way it was dried and stored. This unit explains why herbal quality control is different, the WHO "basic tests" for checking drugs when a full laboratory is not available, the WHO methods for quality control of herbal materials, and how commercial crude drugs are evaluated before use.

## 1.1 Why quality control of herbals is special

| Problem | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| **Natural variation** | Constituent content changes with genotype, soil, climate, altitude, age of plant, time and season of collection |
| **Complex make-up** | Many constituents act together; the active one may be unknown, so no single assay proves quality |
| **Adulteration and substitution** | Look-alike plants, exhausted drugs, cheaper species, wrong plant part, deliberate mixing |
| **Contamination** | Pesticide residues, heavy metals, microbes, aflatoxins, radioactive matter, foreign matter |
| **Processing changes** | Drying, storage and extraction alter content; volatile oils and enzymes are lost or activated |
| **Multi-ingredient products** | Classical Ayurvedic formulations often contain many herbs; identifying each one in the finished product is hard |

So herbal quality control rests on three questions, asked at every stage from field to finished pack:

```text
   IDENTITY            PURITY                  CONTENT / STRENGTH
 Is it the right   Is it free from foreign    Does it contain enough of
 plant and part?   matter and contaminants?   its marker or active constituents?
        \                  |                        /
         \_________________|_______________________/
                           |
                    SAFETY + CONSISTENCY
              (same quality batch after batch)
```

### Key definitions (WHO usage)

- **Herbs** — crude plant material: leaves, flowers, fruits, seeds, stems, wood, bark, roots, rhizomes or other parts, whole, fragmented or powdered.
- **Herbal materials** — herbs plus fresh juices, gums, fixed oils, essential oils, resins and dry powders of herbs.
- **Herbal preparations** — the basis of finished products: comminuted or powdered herbal materials, extracts, tinctures and fatty oils, made by extraction, fractionation, purification, concentration or other processes.
- **Finished herbal products** — herbal preparations made from one or more herbs; may contain excipients.
- **Quality control** — the testing of materials and products against specifications, with the sampling and release procedures needed.
- **Standardisation** — setting and applying specifications (identity, purity, content) so that every batch of a herbal drug is of uniform, defined quality. For extracts it often means adjusting the extract to a stated content of constituents.

## 1.2 Basic tests for drugs

WHO published **"Basic tests for drugs"** in separate volumes for **pharmaceutical substances**, **medicinal plant materials** and **dosage forms**. They are simple tests that can be done with few reagents and simple equipment — even outside a fully equipped laboratory — by a pharmacist or trained technician.

### Purpose

1. To **confirm the identity** of a drug or plant material when a full pharmacopoeial analysis is not possible.
2. To **detect gross degradation** or obvious substandard material.
3. To **screen** suspect samples in the supply chain (warehouses, hospital stores, remote areas) and pick out those that must go to a full quality control laboratory.

### Main features

- Use readily available reagents and simple apparatus (test tubes, water-bath, hand lens, simple TLC).
- Each test is short and gives a clear yes/no result.
- They **do not replace** pharmacopoeial testing. A sample that passes a basic test is not proven to be of full pharmacopoeial quality; a sample that fails must be fully analysed before action is taken.

### What the tests look at

| Material | Typical basic tests |
| --- | --- |
| **Pharmaceutical substances** | Appearance, colour, odour; solubility; simple colour or precipitation reactions for functional groups and ions; melting behaviour; simple TLC against a reference |
| **Medicinal plant materials** | Macroscopic features (shape, size, colour, surface, fracture); odour and taste; microscopy of the powder; simple chemical tests (for alkaloids, tannins, saponins, anthraquinones); fluorescence under UV; simple TLC |
| **Dosage forms** | Visual inspection (colour, cracks, mottling, discoloration); identity of the active by colour reaction or TLC; simple disintegration check; signs of degradation such as smell of acetic acid from aspirin tablets |

## 1.3 WHO guidelines for quality control of herbal drugs

WHO first published **"Quality control methods for medicinal plant materials"** (1998); it was updated as **"Quality control methods for herbal materials"** (2011). It is **not a pharmacopoeia**. It is a collection of test methods that countries can use to build their own national standards. Alongside it, WHO issued **"Guidelines for assessing quality of herbal medicines with reference to contaminants and residues"** (2007), which gives examples of national limits.

### Tests described in the WHO manual

```text
 General notices -> Powder fineness and sieve size -> Sampling
 Foreign matter -> Macroscopy and microscopy -> Thin-layer chromatography
 Ash (total, acid-insoluble, water-soluble) -> Extractable matter
 Water and volatile matter -> Volatile oils -> Bitterness value
 Haemolytic activity -> Tannins -> Swelling index -> Foaming index
 Pesticide residues -> Arsenic and toxic metals -> Microorganisms
 Aflatoxins -> Radioactive contamination
```

### Sampling

Herbal material is not uniform, so the sample must represent the whole batch.

- **Batch of up to 5 containers** — sample every container.
- **6–50 containers** — sample 5.
- **More than 50** — sample 10%, rounding up to the nearest multiple of 10 (51 units are sampled as 60, i.e. 6 packages).
- From each selected container take **three original samples** — top, middle and bottom. In sacks the first sample is taken from not less than 10 cm deep.
- Combine to a **pooled sample**, mix, and reduce by **quartering**: spread in a square heap, divide diagonally into four, keep two opposite quarters, mix and repeat until the required amount remains.
- Divide the average sample into **final samples** for testing and keep a portion as a **retained (reference) sample**.

### Foreign matter

Herbal materials should be free from visible moulds, insects and animal contamination, and from poisonous foreign matter. Foreign matter means other parts of the same plant beyond the stated limit, other organisms, and mineral admixtures (soil, stones, sand, dust). Sample sizes: **500 g** for roots, rhizomes and bark; **250 g** for leaves, flowers, seeds and fruits; **50 g** for cut material. The sample is spread thin, sorted with a hand lens (6× or 10×), and each group weighed and expressed in g per 100 g.

### Macroscopic and microscopic examination

Identity is first checked by shape, size, colour, surface, texture, fracture, odour and taste, compared with a reference specimen. Microscopy of sections and powder shows diagnostic features — stomata type, trichomes, calcium oxalate crystals, starch grains, fibres, vessels, stone cells. Microscopy is indispensable for powders.

### Ash values

| Ash | How it is obtained | What it shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Total ash** | 2–4 g ignited at 500–600 °C until white (carbon-free) | Physiological ash of the tissue plus non-physiological ash from adhering earth |
| **Acid-insoluble ash** | Total ash boiled with dilute HCl, insoluble matter ignited | Silica — sand and earthy matter |
| **Water-soluble ash** | Total ash boiled with water; weight lost on washing | Water-soluble inorganic matter; low in exhausted drugs |
| **Sulphated ash** | Ignition after treating with sulphuric acid | Used for some drugs and pure substances |

### Extractable matter (extractive values)

Used where no reliable chemical assay exists; it measures the amount of constituents extracted by a solvent.

- **Hot extraction** — 4 g of coarse powder refluxed with 100 ml of solvent for 1 hour, cooled, made up to the original weight, filtered; 25 ml of filtrate evaporated, dried at 105 °C for 6 hours and weighed.
- **Cold maceration** — 4 g macerated with 100 ml solvent for 6 hours with shaking, left 18 hours, filtered; 25 ml evaporated and dried at 105 °C.
- Solvents: water (water-soluble extractive), ethanol of stated strength (alcohol-soluble extractive), or others as specified. Low values point to exhausted or adulterated drug.

### Water and volatile matter

- **Azeotropic (toluene distillation)** method — the sample is distilled with water-saturated toluene; water collects in a graduated receiver. Measures water directly, so it is preferred for drugs with volatile oils.
- **Loss on drying** — drying at 100–105 °C, or in a desiccator over phosphorus pentoxide, until two weighings differ by not more than 5 mg; measures water plus volatile matter.

Excess water allows microbial growth, mould, insects and hydrolysis, so a limit is set for each material.

### Special tests

| Test | Principle | Example use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Volatile oil** | Steam distillation in a Clevenger-type apparatus; oil read in a graduated tube | Clove, cinnamon, eucalyptus |
| **Bitterness value** | Threshold bitter concentration of an extract compared with quinine hydrochloride; one unit = bitterness of 1 g quinine hydrochloride in 2000 ml | Gentian, chirata, neem |
| **Haemolytic activity** | Saponins lyse red blood cells; compared with reference saponin | Saponin drugs (liquorice, shatavari) |
| **Tannins** | Tannins bind to hide powder; difference in water-extractable matter before and after hide powder | Catechu, myrobalan |
| **Swelling index** | Volume (ml) occupied by 1 g of drug after swelling in water in a 25 ml cylinder (shaken every 10 min for 1 h, left 3 h) | Isabgol, linseed, fenugreek |
| **Foaming index** | Decoction (1 g in 100 ml) diluted in 10 tubes, shaken, foam measured after 15 min; index = 1000/a, where a = ml of decoction in the tube giving 1 cm foam | Saponin drugs |

### Contaminants

**Pesticide residues** — organochlorine, organophosphorus and pyrethroid residues are extracted, cleaned up and measured, mostly by gas chromatography. National limits are set from the **acceptable daily intake (ADI)** of the pesticide and the **mean daily intake** of the herb.

**Arsenic and toxic metals** — arsenic by limit test or atomic absorption; lead and cadmium by atomic absorption spectroscopy or ICP; a limit test for total toxic metals as lead. WHO has suggested maximum limits of **lead 10 mg/kg** and **cadmium 0.3 mg/kg** in herbal materials; other limits are set nationally.

**Microorganisms** — total viable aerobic count, yeasts and moulds, and tests for specific organisms (*Escherichia coli*, *Salmonella*, *Staphylococcus aureus*, *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, other enterobacteria).

**Aflatoxins** — toxins (B1, B2, G1, G2) of *Aspergillus flavus* and related moulds on poorly dried or badly stored material. The WHO method uses a clean-up column and HPLC with fluorescence detection. Only materials with a history of aflatoxin contamination need routine testing.

**Radioactive contamination** — after nuclear accidents; measured by national radiation laboratories.

### Limits

WHO states that it **cannot recommend single international limits** for contaminants, because they vary too much and there is no consensus. Instead it gives test methods and **examples of national limits**, to be used as a basis for national standards. Examples from the WHO 2007 contaminants guideline:

| Category of herbal material or medicine | Aerobic bacteria (max per g) | Yeasts and moulds (max per g) | *E. coli* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-treated with boiling water (teas, infusions) or used topically | 10^7 | 10^4 | 10^2 per g |
| Other herbal materials for internal use | 10^5 | 10^3 | 10 per g |
| Other (finished) herbal medicines | 10^5 | 10^3 | Absent in 1 g |

In all these categories *Salmonella*, *Shigella* and clostridia must be absent in 1 g. For aflatoxins, Germany's limit quoted by WHO is **2 µg/kg for aflatoxin B1** and **4 µg/kg for the sum of B1, B2, G1 and G2**.

**Setting a limit from data**: WHO suggests pooling results of about **20 successive batches** and using the grand average ± **three standard deviations** ("three sigma limits").

## 1.4 Evaluation of commercial crude drugs intended for use

**Evaluation** is the confirmation of identity and the determination of quality and purity of a crude drug. Commercial samples are bought in bulk from traders, so they must be checked before use in manufacture.

### Methods of evaluation

| Method | What is done | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Organoleptic** (morphological) | Colour, odour, taste, size, shape, surface, fracture | Fibrous fracture of quassia; aromatic odour of clove; bitter taste of chirata |
| **Microscopic** | Sections and powder; histochemical stains; quantitative microscopy | Stomatal index, palisade ratio, vein-islet and vein-termination number |
| **Physical** | Moisture, ash, extractives, swelling, foaming, solubility, viscosity, optical rotation, refractive index, melting point | Refractive index of volatile oils; viscosity of gums |
| **Chemical** | Identity tests and assays of constituents or groups | Borntrager's test (anthraquinones); alkaloid assay; acid value of resins |
| **Chromatographic / spectroscopic** | TLC/HPTLC fingerprint, HPLC assay of markers, UV, IR | Sennosides in senna, curcuminoids in turmeric |
| **Biological** | Bioassay of potency when chemistry is inadequate | Cardiac glycosides (historically), antimicrobial activity |

### Quantitative microscopy (leaf constants)

- **Stomatal number** — average number of stomata per sq mm of epidermis.
- **Stomatal index** — SI = S × 100 / (E + S), where S = stomata and E = epidermal cells per unit area; fairly constant for a species.
- **Palisade ratio** — average number of palisade cells beneath one epidermal cell.
- **Vein-islet number** — number of vein islets per sq mm of leaf surface (midway between midrib and margin).
- **Vein-termination number** — number of vein terminations per sq mm.
- **Lycopodium spore method** — used to estimate the percentage of a powdered drug, or of an adulterant, when it has a countable characteristic element (starch grains, pollen, fibres). Lycopodium spores are uniform in size and number per milligram, so they act as an internal standard.

### Adulteration of crude drugs

**Adulteration** is the debasement of a drug by admixture, substitution or removal of constituents. Types:

1. **Substitution with inferior commercial varieties** — for example, Indian senna sold as Alexandrian senna; Japanese ginger for Jamaica ginger.
2. **Substitution by exhausted drug** — already-extracted ginger, clove or coffee dried and resold; detected by low extractive or volatile oil values.
3. **Substitution with superficially similar but cheaper plants** — related species, or wrong plant parts (stems mixed with leaves).
4. **Substitution with artificially manufactured material** — moulded imitation nutmegs, artificial seeds.
5. **Adding synthetic principles** — synthetic citral to lemon oil, synthetic benzyl benzoate to balsams.
6. **Use of vegetative parts of the same plant** in place of the official part.
7. **Addition of worthless heavy materials** — sand, stones, lead shot in opium, limestone.
8. **Use of harmful or spoiled drug** — mouldy, insect-infested or decayed material.

Reasons for adulteration include scarcity, high price, confusion of vernacular names, lack of knowledge of authentic plants, and careless collection or storage.

### Workflow for a commercial crude drug

```text
Receipt -> quarantine -> sampling (WHO plan)
   -> identity: macroscopy, microscopy, TLC/HPTLC fingerprint
   -> purity: foreign matter, ash values, moisture
   -> content: extractives, volatile oil, marker assay
   -> safety: pesticides, heavy metals, microbes, aflatoxins
   -> pass: released to production    fail: rejected and recorded
```

## Remember

- Quality = identity + purity + content, plus safety and batch-to-batch consistency.
- WHO "Basic tests for drugs" — simple tests for substances, plant materials and dosage forms; confirm identity and detect gross degradation; never replace pharmacopoeial analysis.
- WHO QC methods manual (1998, updated 2011) is a set of test methods, not a pharmacopoeia.
- Sampling: up to 5 containers all; 6–50 take 5; above 50 take 10% (rounded up to a multiple of 10); top, middle, bottom; reduce by quartering.
- Foreign matter samples: 500 g roots/bark, 250 g leaves/flowers/seeds/fruits, 50 g cut material.
- Total ash 500–600 °C; acid-insoluble ash = silica/sand; water-soluble ash low in exhausted drugs.
- Water: toluene distillation (direct water) versus loss on drying (water + volatiles).
- Bitterness unit = 1 g quinine hydrochloride in 2000 ml; foaming index = 1000/a; swelling index in ml per g.
- WHO-suggested heavy-metal limits: lead 10 mg/kg, cadmium 0.3 mg/kg. WHO gives examples of national limits, not single global limits.
- Microbial examples: teas/topical 10^7 aerobic bacteria per g; other internal herbal materials 10^5; *Salmonella* and *Shigella* absent.
- Stomatal index = S × 100/(E + S); lycopodium spore method for quantitative microscopy of powders.

# Unit 2: Quality assurance in the herbal industry — GAP, GACP, GMP, cGMP and GLP

Testing at the end cannot put quality into a herbal medicine. If the wrong plant was collected, if it was dried on the roadside and grew mould, or if a mixer was not cleaned after the previous batch, no laboratory test can rescue the product. Quality must be **built in** at every step: in the field (good agricultural and collection practices), in the factory (good manufacturing practices) and in the test laboratory (good laboratory practice). This unit covers these systems as they apply to herbal medicines and the traditional systems of medicine, with special attention to the two WHO guidelines named in the syllabus.

## 2.1 Quality assurance, GMP and quality control

```text
            QUALITY ASSURANCE (QA)
   the total system that makes sure products are of the
   quality required for their intended use
                     |
           GOOD MANUFACTURING PRACTICE (GMP)
   the part of QA that makes sure products are consistently
   produced and controlled to suitable quality standards
                     |
              QUALITY CONTROL (QC)
   the part of GMP concerned with sampling, specifications,
   testing, and release or rejection of materials and products
```

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Quality assurance** | Organised arrangements covering design, development, production, control, distribution and complaint handling, so that every product reaching the patient is fit for use |
| **GMP** | Rules for premises, equipment, personnel, materials, processes and records in manufacturing |
| **cGMP** | "Current" GMP — the expectation that manufacturers use up-to-date technology and systems, not just the minimum written years ago |
| **GAP / GACP** | Good agricultural (and collection) practices for growing and collecting medicinal plants |
| **GLP** | Good laboratory practice — a quality system for non-clinical safety studies (toxicity and similar tests) |
| **GCP** | Good clinical practice — for clinical trials (Unit 3) |

### Why QA is harder for herbal products

- The starting material is a **living, variable** plant, not a pure chemical.
- **Contamination risks** begin in the field — pesticides, heavy metals from soil, microbes from manure and water, mould during drying.
- **Identification** needs botanical skill; look-alike species and trade names cause confusion.
- Herbal powders produce **dust**, which carries cross-contamination, microbes and a fire/explosion risk.
- Materials are bulky and **hygroscopic**; insects and rodents are a constant threat in stores.
- Specifications often rely on **fingerprints and markers** instead of a single assay.

## 2.2 Good agricultural practice (GAP) and WHO guidelines on GACP for medicinal plants

**WHO guidelines on Good Agricultural and Collection Practices (GACP) for medicinal plants** (2003) give guidance for both cultivated and wild-collected plants. Their aims are to:

1. Improve the **quality, safety and efficacy** of herbal medicines at the source.
2. Guide countries in making their own GACP guidelines and monographs.
3. Encourage **sustainable** cultivation and collection that protects plant species and the environment, and respects the rights of local communities.

In India, the **National Medicinal Plants Board (NMPB)** has issued GACP guidelines for medicinal plants based on the WHO guidelines.

### Main sections of WHO GACP

| Section | Key points |
| --- | --- |
| **Identification and authentication** | Botanical name (genus, species, author) and family; local names; **voucher specimen** deposited in a herbarium; identity confirmed by a botanist |
| **Seeds and propagation material** | Authentic species and variety; pure, free from pests and diseases; organic seed where possible |
| **Cultivation — site selection** | Soil and water free from heavy metals, pesticide residues and other contaminants; past land use known |
| **Climate and soil** | Suitable for the species, since climate and soil affect constituent content |
| **Irrigation and fertilisation** | Water of suitable quality; manure well composted to avoid microbial load; no human excreta |
| **Crop maintenance and protection** | Minimum pesticide use; integrated pest management; only approved agents, at permitted doses, recorded |
| **Harvest** | At the best season and time of day for constituent content; dry weather; clean tools; damaged and foreign plants removed; no contact with soil |
| **Collection (wild plants)** | Permission from authorities; no endangered species; sustainable methods leaving enough plants to regenerate; trained collectors |
| **Primary processing** | Prompt inspection and sorting; washing only if allowed; drying (sun, shade, or dryer) on clean surfaces, protected from animals and dust; specific treatments (peeling, slicing, fermentation) |
| **Packaging and labelling** | Clean, dry containers; label with botanical name, part, origin, date, batch |
| **Storage and transport** | Dry, ventilated, pest-proof stores; separate from other goods; fumigation only with permitted agents and recorded |
| **Equipment** | Clean, easy to maintain; does not contaminate |
| **Personnel** | Trained; healthy; personal hygiene; protective clothing when handling toxic or allergenic plants |
| **Documentation** | Records of seed source, site, cultivation inputs, pesticides used, harvest date, processing, batch numbers — so every batch can be traced |
| **Quality assurance** | Agreements on quality between producer and buyer; audits |
| **Ethical and legal issues** | Intellectual property, benefit sharing with local communities, protection of threatened species |

```text
 Seed -> Site -> Cultivation -> Harvest/Collection -> Primary processing
      -> Packaging -> Storage -> Transport -> Manufacturer (quarantine)
   (documents travel with every batch: traceability from field to factory)
```

**Benefits of GACP** — consistent raw material, lower contamination, fewer rejected batches, traceability, acceptance in export markets, and conservation of wild resources.

## 2.3 Good manufacturing practice for herbal medicines

### WHO guidelines on GMP for herbal medicines

WHO published supplementary **guidelines on good manufacturing practices (GMP) for herbal medicines** (2007). They do not replace the main WHO GMP text; they add the points that are specific to herbal materials. The headings follow general GMP, with herbal-specific detail:

| Area | Herbal-specific requirements |
| --- | --- |
| **Quality assurance** | Herbal materials and preparations handled as "starting materials"; supplier qualification and audits of farms and collectors where possible |
| **Sanitation and hygiene** | Plant material carries soil and microbes; separate areas for receipt, cleaning and storage of raw herbs |
| **Qualification and validation** | Validation of cleaning, extraction, drying and sterilising or decontaminating processes |
| **Complaints and recalls** | Records allow tracing back to the herbal batch and its source |
| **Contract production and analysis** | Written contracts; clear responsibilities |
| **Self-inspection** | Regular internal audits |
| **Personnel** | Trained in botany/pharmacognosy as well as GMP; protection from dust and allergenic or toxic plants |
| **Premises** | Raw herbs stored apart from processed materials and finished products; well ventilated, pest-proof; **dust extraction** where powders are cut, ground, sieved or mixed; separate quarantine areas |
| **Equipment** | Easy to clean; dedicated equipment where cross-contamination is a risk |
| **Materials** | Quarantine on receipt; sampling; **reference samples and voucher specimens** retained; storage that protects from moisture, light, insects and rodents |
| **Documentation** | Specifications for herbal materials, herbal preparations and finished products; batch processing records; standard operating procedures |
| **Good practices in production** | Defined processing (cutting, drying, extraction); fixed solvents and ratios; mixing of batches only when documented; in-process controls |
| **Good practices in quality control** | Identity by macroscopy, microscopy and fingerprint; tests for contaminants; stability; retention of samples |

### What a specification for a herbal material should state

1. **Botanical name** (genus, species, variety, author) and family.
2. **Source** — country or region; cultivated or wild; time of collection; pre-treatment (drying, fumigation).
3. **Part used** and whether fresh or dried, whole or powdered.
4. **Description** — macroscopic and microscopic features.
5. **Identity tests** — chemical tests and a **TLC/HPTLC fingerprint** against a reference.
6. **Assay** — content of active constituents or markers, with limits.
7. **Purity tests** — foreign matter, total and acid-insoluble ash, moisture, extractive values.
8. **Contaminant tests** — pesticides, heavy metals, microbes, aflatoxins, residual fumigants or solvents, radioactivity where relevant.
9. **Other tests** — particle size, swelling index, volatile oil.
10. **Storage conditions** and re-test period.

For **herbal preparations (extracts)** the specification adds the solvent used, the **drug-to-extract ratio**, residual solvent limits and, where relevant, the content range of markers.

### cGMP — keeping GMP current

"Current" means the manufacturer keeps its quality system up to date with modern methods: validated processes, computerised records with audit trails, risk-based thinking, environmental monitoring, change control, deviation and CAPA (corrective and preventive action) systems, and periodic product quality review. Inspectors judge a plant against what is current practice today.

## 2.4 GMP in the traditional systems of medicine (India)

In India, Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani (ASU) medicines are manufactured under licence, and the licence requires compliance with **Schedule T** of the **Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945** — the GMP for ASU medicines (studied in detail in Herbal Drug Technology, sixth semester). Its main headings:

```text
Schedule T, Part I (GMP requirements)
  premises and location  -> water supply -> waste disposal
  container cleaning     -> stores (raw material, packing, finished goods, quarantine)
  working space          -> health, clothing and sanitation of workers
  medical services       -> machinery and equipment
  batch manufacturing records -> distribution records
  record of market complaints and adverse reactions -> quality control
Schedule T, Part II
  list of machinery and minimum manufacturing area for each ASU dosage form
```

Points that bring Indian ASU units in line with WHO GMP:

- **Raw material store** with separate sections for herbs, minerals and animal products; poisonous drugs (listed in Schedule E(1)) kept separately and under lock.
- **Authentication** of every raw herb by a qualified person before release.
- **Quality control** section, or approved testing laboratories, to test raw materials and finished products against pharmacopoeial standards.
- **Batch manufacturing records** that allow full traceability.
- **WHO-GMP certification** of ASU units, needed by many export markets, is granted after inspection against WHO GMP for herbal medicines.

## 2.5 Good laboratory practice (GLP)

**GLP** is a quality system covering the **organisational process and the conditions** under which **non-clinical health and environmental safety studies** are planned, performed, monitored, recorded, archived and reported. It ensures that the toxicity data submitted to regulators are reliable and can be reconstructed. The internationally accepted text is the **OECD Principles of GLP**. In India, laboratories are inspected and certified by the **National GLP Compliance Monitoring Authority (NGCMA)** under the Department of Science and Technology.

### OECD principles of GLP

| Principle | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **Test facility organisation and personnel** | Management responsibilities; a **study director** responsible for each study; qualified, trained staff |
| **Quality assurance programme** | An independent QA unit inspects studies and audits reports |
| **Facilities** | Suitable size and design; separate areas for test systems (animals), test items, archives and waste |
| **Apparatus, materials and reagents** | Calibrated, maintained, labelled with identity and expiry |
| **Test systems** | Proper housing and care of animals or other systems; records of receipt and health |
| **Test and reference items** | Characterised; identity, batch, purity, stability and storage recorded |
| **Standard operating procedures** | Written SOPs for every routine activity |
| **Performance of the study** | Written **study plan (protocol)** approved by the study director; raw data recorded promptly and signed |
| **Reporting of results** | Final report with methods, results and a QA statement |
| **Storage and retention of records** | Archives for protocols, raw data, specimens and reports |

### Why GLP matters for herbal drugs

- Toxicity studies of herbal extracts and phytopharmaceuticals submitted for approval must be done in **GLP-compliant** laboratories to be accepted by regulators, including in export markets.
- The **test item** must be a fully characterised herbal extract — botanical identity, extraction method, drug-to-extract ratio, fingerprint and marker content — so that the safety result applies to a defined product.
- GLP also guides quality control laboratories in documentation, calibration and data integrity, even when formal certification is not required.

## 2.6 Documents that support quality assurance

| Document | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| **Standard operating procedure (SOP)** | Step-by-step instructions for a routine task (cleaning a pulveriser, sampling herbs) |
| **Master formula record** | Approved formula and method for a product: ingredients, quantities, process, equipment, in-process checks |
| **Batch manufacturing record** | What actually happened for one batch, signed at each step |
| **Specifications** | Tests and limits for raw materials, intermediates, finished products |
| **Certificate of analysis** | Test results for a batch released by QC |
| **Validation protocols and reports** | Evidence that processes and methods do what they claim |
| **Deviation, change control and CAPA records** | Investigation and correction of departures from procedure |

## Remember

- QA ⊃ GMP ⊃ QC. cGMP = current, up-to-date GMP.
- WHO GACP for medicinal plants (2003): identification with voucher specimen, seed, site, cultivation, harvest, collection, primary processing, packaging, storage, personnel, documentation, ethics.
- WHO GMP for herbal medicines (2007) is supplementary to main GMP: separate raw-herb storage, dust control, voucher and reference samples, fingerprint-based specifications, contaminant testing.
- Herbal material specification: botanical name, source, part, description, identity (TLC fingerprint), assay, purity, contaminants, storage.
- ASU GMP in India = Schedule T (Part I requirements, Part II machinery and area); poisonous ASU ingredients in Schedule E(1).
- GLP = OECD principles for non-clinical safety studies: study director, QA unit, SOPs, study plan, raw data, archives. India: NGCMA under DST.

# Unit 3: EU and ICH guidelines and research guidelines for safety and efficacy

Indian herbal products are sold in Europe, the USA and many other countries, and Indian companies that export must meet the standards of those markets. The European Union has the most developed system for herbal medicines, and the ICH guidelines set the technical rules that regulators worldwide expect. This unit covers the EU framework, the ICH guidelines that apply to herbal products, and the WHO research guidelines for proving that a herbal medicine is safe and effective.

## 3.1 The European Union framework for herbal medicinal products

### Bodies and laws

| Item | Role |
| --- | --- |
| **European Medicines Agency (EMA)** | EU agency for scientific evaluation of medicines |
| **Committee on Herbal Medicinal Products (HMPC)** | Scientific committee of EMA for herbal medicines; prepares EU herbal monographs, the list of herbal substances for traditional use, and quality and safety guidelines |
| **Directive 2001/83/EC** | The basic EU law for medicinal products for human use |
| **Directive 2004/24/EC** | Amended Directive 2001/83/EC to create the **simplified registration of traditional herbal medicinal products** |
| **European Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Eur.)** | Legally binding quality standards, including general and individual monographs for herbal drugs, preparations and extracts |

### EU definitions

- **Herbal substance** — whole, fragmented or cut plants, plant parts, algae, fungi or lichens, in unprocessed form, usually dried but sometimes fresh. Defined by the plant part used and the full botanical name.
- **Herbal preparation** — obtained by treating a herbal substance: extraction, distillation, expression, fractionation, purification, concentration or fermentation. Includes powders, tinctures, extracts, essential oils, expressed juices and exudates.
- **Herbal medicinal product** — any medicinal product containing as active ingredients only herbal substances, herbal preparations, or both.

In the EU the **whole herbal substance or preparation is treated as the active substance**, even when individual constituents with known activity are measured.

### Three routes to the EU market

| Route | Evidence needed | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Full marketing authorisation** (stand-alone application) | Own quality, non-clinical and clinical data, as for any new drug | New herbal products with new claims |
| **Well-established use** (bibliographic application) | Published scientific literature showing **well-established medicinal use** in the EU for at least 10 years, with recognised efficacy and acceptable safety; full quality data | Senna for constipation, ispaghula, St John's wort extracts with clinical evidence |
| **Traditional use registration** (simplified, Directive 2004/24/EC) | **Evidence of traditional use for at least 30 years, including at least 15 years within the EU**; bibliographic review of safety; efficacy is accepted as plausible from long use; **full quality data still required** | Products for minor, self-limiting conditions |

Conditions for traditional use registration:

1. Indications suitable for use **without a doctor's supervision** for diagnosis, prescription or monitoring.
2. **Oral, external or inhalation** use only.
3. A specified strength and posology.
4. The 30-year/15-year period of traditional use.
5. Data on traditional use show the product is **not harmful** under the stated conditions, and its pharmacological effects or efficacy are **plausible** from long use.

Labels of such products state that the product is a traditional herbal medicinal product for use in the stated indications **exclusively based on long-standing use**.

### EU herbal monographs and the list

- **EU herbal monographs** (earlier "Community herbal monographs") summarise the HMPC's view on a herbal substance or preparation: well-established and/or traditional use, indications, posology, contraindications, warnings, interactions, adverse effects.
- **The EU list** of herbal substances, preparations and combinations for traditional use: an applicant whose product matches a list entry need not prove traditional use or safety separately.

### EU quality guidelines for herbal products

EMA/HMPC quality guidelines cover:

1. **Quality of herbal medicinal products and traditional herbal medicinal products** — what must be described in the dossier for the herbal substance, herbal preparation and finished product.
2. **Specifications: test procedures and acceptance criteria** for herbal substances, herbal preparations and herbal medicinal products.
3. **Good agricultural and collection practice (GACP)** for starting materials of herbal origin.
4. **Stability testing** of herbal products, with markers and fingerprints.
5. **Declaration of herbal substances and preparations** on labels.

#### What the quality dossier must cover

| Stage | Information |
| --- | --- |
| **Herbal substance** | Botanical name, part, geographical source, cultivated or wild, harvest, drying, storage; GACP; specification with identity (macroscopy, microscopy, chromatographic fingerprint), purity (foreign matter, ash, water), contaminants (pesticides, fumigants, heavy metals, mycotoxins, microbial quality, radioactivity where relevant) |
| **Herbal preparation** | Manufacturing process, **extraction solvent**, **drug–extract ratio (DER)**, excipients added; specification with fingerprint, marker content, residual solvents |
| **Finished product** | Composition, manufacture, controls, validation, container, **stability** |

**Drug–extract ratio (DER)** — ratio of the quantity of herbal substance used to the quantity of extract obtained. A DER of 4–6:1 means 4 to 6 kg of dried herb gives 1 kg of native extract.

#### Types of extracts (Ph. Eur. classification)

| Type | Definition | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Standardised extract** | Adjusted to a defined content of constituents with **known therapeutic activity**, using excipients or by mixing batches; content stated as a single value with tolerance | Senna leaf dry extract adjusted to a stated content of hydroxyanthracene glycosides |
| **Quantified extract** | Adjusted to a defined **range** of constituents (often active markers) whose contribution to activity is accepted but not proven alone, by mixing batches | Ginkgo leaf extract with stated ranges of flavone glycosides and terpene lactones |
| **Other extracts** | Not adjusted; defined by production process (herb, solvent, DER) and by specification, using **analytical markers** for control | Many extracts of herbs whose actives are unknown |

#### Markers in EU usage

**Markers** are chemically defined constituents or groups of constituents used for control purposes, whether or not they have therapeutic activity.

- **Active markers** — contribute to the therapeutic activity.
- **Analytical markers** — used only to check identity, quality and consistency.

## 3.2 ICH guidelines and herbal drugs

The **International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use (ICH)** brings together regulators and industry to agree technical guidelines. ICH has **no guideline written only for herbal products**, but its quality, safety, efficacy and multidisciplinary guidelines are applied to herbal products and extracts, especially in dossiers for regulated markets.

| ICH guideline | Subject | How it is used for herbals |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Q1A(R2)** | Stability testing of new drug substances and products | Storage conditions and test frequency for extracts and finished herbal products |
| **Q1B** | Photostability testing | Light-sensitive constituents (hypericin, curcuminoids, chlorophyll) |
| **Q2** | Validation of analytical procedures | Validating HPLC/HPTLC methods for markers, fingerprints, pesticides |
| **Q3C** | Residual solvents (classes 1, 2, 3) | Solvents left in extracts — hexane, methanol, ethanol, acetone |
| **Q3D** | Elemental impurities | Risk assessment for lead, cadmium, arsenic, mercury |
| **Q6A** | Specifications for chemical substances and products | Approach to setting tests and acceptance criteria, adapted for herbal products |
| **Q7** | GMP for active pharmaceutical ingredients | Manufacture of herbal extracts used as active ingredients |
| **Q8, Q9, Q10** | Pharmaceutical development, quality risk management, pharmaceutical quality system | Designing robust extraction processes; risk-based control of contamination |
| **M4 (CTD)** | Common Technical Document format | Modules 1–5 for registration dossiers |
| **S-series** | Non-clinical safety studies (genotoxicity, reproductive toxicity, safety pharmacology and others) | Safety studies of new herbal drugs and phytopharmaceuticals |
| **E6** | Good clinical practice | Clinical trials of herbal medicines |

### ICH stability conditions (Q1A(R2))

| Study | Storage condition | Minimum period at submission |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Long-term | 25 °C ± 2 °C / 60% RH ± 5% RH, or 30 °C ± 2 °C / 65% RH ± 5% RH | 12 months |
| Intermediate | 30 °C ± 2 °C / 65% RH ± 5% RH | 6 months |
| Accelerated | 40 °C ± 2 °C / 75% RH ± 5% RH | 6 months |

India is in the hot and very humid **climatic zone IVb**, for which WHO guidance uses **30 °C / 75% RH** as the long-term condition (details in Unit 4).

### Common Technical Document (CTD)

```text
Module 1  Regional administrative information (country-specific)
Module 2  Summaries: quality overall summary, non-clinical and clinical overviews
Module 3  Quality (herbal substance, preparation, finished product)
Module 4  Non-clinical study reports
Module 5  Clinical study reports
```

## 3.3 Research guidelines for evaluating the safety and efficacy of herbal medicines

WHO (through its Regional Office for the Western Pacific) published **"Research guidelines for evaluating the safety and efficacy of herbal medicines"**, and later the **"General guidelines for methodologies on research and evaluation of traditional medicine"** (2000). Their aim is to help countries ask for the right amount of evidence — not ignoring long traditional experience, but not accepting claims without proof.

### General principles

1. **Quality comes first.** The material tested must be botanically identified and standardised; otherwise results cannot be repeated or applied to the marketed product.
2. **Traditional use is evidence.** A herb used for a long time without reports of harm, in the same preparation and dose, may need fewer new toxicity studies.
3. **New is new.** A new indication, a new preparation (for example a concentrated extract instead of a decoction), a new route, a higher dose or a new combination requires fresh safety and efficacy data.
4. **Ethics** — research on humans follows the Declaration of Helsinki, approval by an ethics committee and informed consent.

### Evaluation of safety

```text
 Literature and traditional-use review
        |
 Quality and characterisation of the test material
        |
 Acute toxicity (single dose)
        |
 Repeated-dose (sub-acute / sub-chronic / chronic) toxicity
   duration linked to the intended duration of clinical use
        |
 Special studies when indicated:
   local tolerance, sensitisation, genotoxicity/mutagenicity,
   carcinogenicity, reproductive and developmental toxicity
        |
 Herb-drug interaction studies (enzymes such as CYP3A4, P-glycoprotein)
        |
 Post-marketing surveillance (pharmacovigilance, Unit 5)
```

- Studies are done in **GLP-compliant** laboratories (Unit 2).
- Observations include body weight, food intake, clinical signs, haematology, biochemistry (liver and kidney function), organ weights and histopathology.
- Special concern for herbs with known toxic groups — pyrrolizidine alkaloids (liver), aristolochic acids (kidney, cancer), and for products containing metals or minerals.

### Evaluation of efficacy

**Pre-clinical (pharmacological) studies** — in vitro tests and animal models that support the traditional claim and suggest a mechanism (anti-inflammatory, hypoglycaemic, hepatoprotective models).

**Clinical trials** — in phases, under good clinical practice:

| Phase | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| I | Safety and tolerability in a small number of volunteers or patients; may be shortened or combined when long traditional use exists |
| II | Efficacy and dose-finding in a small number of patients |
| III | Confirmation of efficacy and safety in larger, randomised, controlled trials |
| IV | Post-marketing studies and surveillance |

Special issues in herbal clinical trials:

- **Placebo design** — herbal products have strong colour, taste and smell, which makes blinding difficult.
- **Individualised treatment** — Ayurveda and traditional Chinese medicine tailor prescriptions to the person (for example by *prakriti*); trial designs must allow for this or test a fixed formula.
- **Outcome measures** — validated modern measures, alongside traditional assessment where relevant.
- **Product consistency** — every batch used in the trial must be standardised and retained.
- **Concomitant medicines** — record them, because of interactions.

### Evidence in India

- **Classical ASU medicines** made as per authoritative books are licensed on the basis of the textual reference; proprietary ASU medicines need evidence of safety and effectiveness; **phytopharmaceutical drugs** need non-clinical and clinical data like new drugs (Unit 4).
- Clinical trials in India follow the **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019**, ICMR ethical guidelines and good clinical practice; the AYUSH research councils (CCRAS, CCRUM, CCRS) carry out and guide research on ASU medicines.

## Remember

- HMPC is the EMA committee for herbal medicines; Directive 2004/24/EC created traditional herbal registration.
- EU routes: full application; well-established use (at least 10 years in the EU, bibliographic); traditional use (30 years, of which 15 in the EU; oral, external or inhalation; no medical supervision needed; full quality data still required).
- EU extract types: standardised (known actives, fixed value), quantified (active markers, range), other (analytical markers).
- Active versus analytical markers; DER = herb : extract.
- ICH has no herbal-only guideline: apply Q1A(R2), Q1B, Q2, Q3C, Q3D, Q6A approach, Q7, Q8–Q10, M4 CTD, S-series, E6.
- ICH stability: long-term 25/60 or 30/65; intermediate 30/65; accelerated 40/75 for 6 months.
- WHO research guidelines: quality first; traditional use counts as evidence; new preparations/indications need new data; acute → repeated-dose → special toxicity; clinical phases I–IV with ethics and GCP.
